overview:
Karuna (kāruṇya, anukampā, dayā) in Jainism is a nuanced ethical and spiritual disposition usually translated as compassion, sympathy, or fellow-feeling toward the suffering of living beings. Unlike some other Indian traditions where compassion is often treated as the central or all-encompassing virtue, Jain thought places karuna within a larger framework dominated by ahiṃsā (non-violence) and the purification of the soul from karmic bondage. Karuna is therefore both deeply valued and carefully analyzed, especially in relation to attachment (rāga), merit (puṇya), and the ultimate goal of liberation (mokṣa).

In classical Jain metaphysics, every living being (jīva) is endowed with consciousness and is subject to pleasure and pain due to the rise of karmic particles. Recognizing this shared vulnerability gives rise to an affective response: distress at the suffering of others and the wish to alleviate it. This is karuna. The Tattvārthasūtra, authoritative for both Digambara and Śvetāmbara traditions, lists kāruṇya among the four bhāvanās (contemplations) that stabilize the vows: maitri (friendliness), pramoda (joy at the virtues of others), kāruṇya (compassion for the afflicted), and mādhyaṣṭya (equanimity toward the ill-behaved. In this context, karuna is a cultivated attitude that supports non-violence and ethical restraint by sensitizing the practitioner to the pain of others and motivating assistance.

At the same time, Jain philosophers distinguish carefully between pure, non-attached states of the soul and those that, while ethically commendable, still involve subtle forms of attachment. Compassion is typically classified as a “beneficial inclination” (śubha parinati) rather than the highest form of dharma. Acharyas note that when one feels sorrow at another’s suffering and acts to relieve it, there is usually some trace of emotional involvement—anukampā as “feeling another’s pain as one’s own.” This generates auspicious karmas (puṇya), which improve future conditions but still bind the soul. Thus, karuna is praised as a powerful force for moral goodness and social care, yet it is not identical with the pure, passionless state required for final liberation.

Jain texts also differentiate types of compassion. A more external, “gross” compassion focuses on physical suffering—hunger, thirst, illness, poverty—and leads to acts such as charity (dāna), medical care, and social service. This is vital for lay practice and is strongly encouraged, especially when directed toward ascetics, the poor, and vulnerable beings. A subtler, more “spiritual” compassion arises in those with some self-knowledge: they grieve over the bondage of souls in saṃsāra and seek to guide others toward right faith, right knowledge, and right conduct. Even this refined compassion, however, is said to retain a very slight trace of rāga, and so remains within the domain of karmic causation.

In everyday Jain life, karuna is expressed through vegetarianism or veganism, careful avoidance of harm to insects and microorganisms, philanthropy, animal protection, and support for education and healthcare. Monastics embody compassion through rigorous observance of ahiṃsā, gentle speech, and teaching that aims to reduce both physical and spiritual suffering. Laypeople cultivate karuna through service (seva), donations, and participation in community welfare projects. Modern Jain ethics often extend this compassion to environmental concerns, advocating for ecological responsibility as an expression of care for all forms of life.

From a doctrinal standpoint, karuna is best understood as an indispensable companion to ahiṃsā rather than its replacement. Compassion without non-violence can become sentimental or partial, while non-violence without compassion risks becoming rigid or indifferent. Jainism therefore integrates karuna into a disciplined path: one first becomes acutely aware of the suffering of beings, responds with compassionate assistance, and gradually refines this response by reducing attachment and ego. In advanced stages (higher guṇasthānas), the practitioner’s relation to others’ suffering becomes increasingly characterized by equanimity and insight, yet the earlier, more affective forms of compassion remain important stepping stones.

Comparatively, Jain karuna shares much with Buddhist karuṇā and Hindu dayā, but its doctrinal placement is distinctive. It is not the sole or supreme virtue; rather, it is one of several key dispositions that support the central Jain commitment to non-violence and spiritual liberation. This careful positioning allows Jain thinkers to affirm the moral necessity of compassion in social and religious life while preserving a rigorous distinction between karmically binding emotions and the passionless purity of the liberated soul.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra 7.11
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: “Friendliness (maitrī) toward all living beings (sattva), joy (pramoda) at the sight of the virtuous (guṇādhika), compassion (kāruṇya) for the afflicted (kliśyamāna), and equanimity (mādhyasthya) toward the ill-behaved (avineya) are the other contemplations (bhāvanās).”
primary_sources.notes: This sūtra is central for understanding karuna as one of the four bhāvanās that stabilize the five vows, especially ahiṃsā. The accompanying Digambara commentary Sarvārthasiddhi by Ācārya Pūjyapāda explains kāruṇya as the disposition to render assistance to those who suffer, highlighting its role as a cultivated attitude that supports ethical practice rather than a purely spontaneous emotion.

primary_sources.title: Tattvārthasūtra 6.12
primary_sources.author: Ācārya Umāsvāti / Umāsvāmi
primary_sources.translation: “Compassion (anukampā) toward living beings (bhūta) in general and toward the devout (vratī) in particular, charity (dāna), restraint-with-attachment (sarāga-saṃyama), and similar practices, together with equanimity (kṣānti) and purity (śauca), are causes of the influx of karmas that produce pleasant feeling (sātā-vedanīya).”
primary_sources.notes: Here compassion is described using the term anukampā and is explicitly linked to the influx of auspicious karmas. This passage shows that even ethically praiseworthy compassion is still within the karmic economy: it generates merit (puṇya) and pleasant experiences but does not itself constitute the passionless state of liberation. It is therefore a śubha parinati, a beneficial but still karmically active inclination.

primary_sources.title: Auto-commentarial tradition on Tattvārthasūtra (maitrī and kāruṇya)
primary_sources.author: Traditional Jain commentators (e.g., Pūjyapāda in Sarvārthasiddhi)
primary_sources.original_text: क्षमेऽहं सर्वसत्त्वानां, क्षमयेऽहं सर्वसत्त्वान्, मैत्री मे सर्वसत्तेषु, वैरं मम न केनचित् ।
primary_sources.transliteration: kṣame ’haṃ sarva-sattvānāṃ, kṣamaye ’haṃ sarva-sattvān, maitrī me sarva-satteṣu, vairaṃ mama na kenacit.
primary_sources.translation: “I forgive all living beings, I ask all living beings for forgiveness, I have friendliness (maitrī) toward all living beings, I have no hostility (vaira) toward anyone.”
primary_sources.notes: This frequently cited passage, associated with the explanation of the bhāvanās, clarifies the relational and affective context in which karuna operates. Maitri and karuna are closely linked to forgiveness and non-hostility, reinforcing the idea that compassion in Jainism is embedded in a broader ethic of reconciliation, restraint, and non-violence.

primary_sources.title: Early Śvetāmbara scriptural usage of karuṇā, dayā, anukampā
primary_sources.author: Canonical Śvetāmbara Jain scriptures ("seniors")
primary_sources.translation: In various early Śvetāmbara texts, terms such as karuṇā, dayā, and anukampā are used to denote compassion, mercy, and sympathetic concern for suffering beings, often in connection with the vows of non-violence and the duties of monks and laypeople.
primary_sources.notes: Scholarly studies of early Jainism show that these terms function as a semantic cluster for compassion, with nuanced differences depending on context. They are frequently invoked in exhortations to protect living beings, to avoid harshness, and to cultivate a gentle, supportive attitude toward those in distress. This corpus underlines that compassion is an integral, though carefully defined, part of Jain ethical vocabulary.

misconceptions.myth: Karuna is the highest and ultimate Jain dharma, identical with liberation itself.
misconceptions.reality: Jainism regards ahiṃsā (non-violence) and the passionless purity of the soul as central to dharma and liberation. Karuna is a highly valued, beneficial inclination that supports non-violence and generates auspicious karmas, but it still involves subtle attachment and therefore remains within the realm of karmic bondage. It is an important step on the path, not the final state of mokṣa.

misconceptions.myth: Compassion in Jainism is purely emotional sympathy and has no structured doctrinal role.
misconceptions.reality: Karuna is systematically integrated into Jain doctrine as one of the four bhāvanās and as a cause of auspicious karmic influx. Texts like the Tattvārthasūtra define and situate compassion within a precise ethical and metaphysical framework. It is not mere sentiment; it is a cultivated disposition that shapes conduct, supports vows, and influences karmic outcomes.

misconceptions.myth: Because compassion can generate karmic merit (puṇya), it is spiritually unnecessary or inferior and should be avoided.
misconceptions.reality: Jain thinkers do not dismiss karuna; they praise it as a śubha parinati that improves conditions for practice, reduces suffering, and strengthens ahiṃsā. While ultimate liberation requires transcending all attachment, including the subtle rāga present in compassion, the path to that state is realistically traversed through stages in which compassionate action and concern for others are indispensable. Avoiding compassion would contradict the core Jain insight into the shared vulnerability of all jīvas.

misconceptions.myth: Karuna in Jainism is limited to human beings and ignores animals, plants, and microscopic life.
misconceptions.reality: Jain compassion extends to all living beings (jīvas), including animals, plants, and even microorganisms. The meticulous practices of monastics—such as wearing mouth-coverings, sweeping the ground, and avoiding root vegetables—are motivated by a combination of ahiṃsā and karuna toward even the smallest forms of life. Lay dietary and ethical rules similarly reflect a broad, inclusive compassion that recognizes the sentience and vulnerability of non-human beings.

misconceptions.myth: Jain karuna is identical to Buddhist karuṇā and can be understood without reference to Jain concepts of karma and ahiṃsā.
misconceptions.reality: While Jain and Buddhist notions of compassion share important similarities, Jain karuna is embedded in a distinct doctrinal matrix centered on non-violence, the multiplicity of souls, and a detailed karmic theory. Understanding Jain compassion requires attention to its role in supporting vows, generating specific karmic results, and coexisting with the ideal of passionless equanimity. Comparative study is fruitful, but it must respect these structural differences.
